headline: A warm Monday in the 60s gives way to a cold, dry Tuesday and Wednesday, then a large coastal storm on Thanksgiving brings 1–2 inches of rain, east-northeast gusts of 35–45 mph (possibly 50 mph at the coast) and widespread coastal flooding.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: Sunday night's low is moving away to the northeast past Montauk, and any lingering light rain on Long Island's North and South Forks should end by daybreak Monday. Monday is dry and still well above normal, with highs in the 60s even as a cold front crosses in the afternoon, bringing west to northwest gusts around 15–20 mph into the evening. Record highs for the date are mostly around 70 (72 at Central Park, 74 at Newark, 70 at LaGuardia), and forecasters think records are unlikely Monday, although Islip has tied or broken its record each of the last four days.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Tuesday and Wednesday turn much colder and stay dry as an unusually strong area of high pressure builds from the Great Lakes into the Northeast. Highs struggle to get out of the 40s, and overnight lows fall mostly below freezing, except in the New York City metro area Wednesday morning. Tuesday brings northwest breezes gusting near 20 mph; clouds thicken Wednesday night, with a slight chance of rain late and east-northeast winds starting to ramp up, especially in the city and along the coast.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: A much larger storm moving north along the East Coast arrives on Thanksgiving Day, and it may track inland, near or just west of the Appalachians, though strong winds are expected either way. The best chance of rain is Thursday afternoon into Thursday night (the immediate coast may see some rain Thursday morning), tapering off early Friday; 1–2 inches looks reasonable, with a 20–30 percent chance of more than 2.5 inches near the coast, falling over about 12–18 hours. East-northeast winds of 20–30 mph gust 35–45 mph, possibly around 50 mph at the coast, strongest Thursday afternoon and evening; there is about a 50–70 percent chance of gusts over 45 mph (advisory level) along the coast and much lower inland. Freshwater flooding should be limited to minor urban and poor-drainage spots because the storm moves through quickly, and on Friday a chance of morning rain remains with west gusts of 25–35 mph as the storm departs.

coast: Coastal flooding is growing more likely Thursday: with a full moon on the 24th and king tides this week, many locations need less than a foot of extra water to reach minor flooding, and the forecast supports widespread minor to moderate coastal flooding, with localized major flooding possible in the most vulnerable spots along the South Shore back bays and western Great South Bay. Beach flooding, erosion and overwash are all possible too. On the water, Small Craft Advisories run until 1 AM Tuesday for Long Island Sound east of the Connecticut River and until 1 PM Tuesday for the nearshore ocean waters, mainly for rough seas, which may linger near 5 feet on the nearshore ocean into early Tuesday afternoon. After a lull late Tuesday into Wednesday, winds ramp up Wednesday night; gales are likely Thursday with possible storm-force winds Thursday and Thursday evening, and peak waves of 15–20 feet on the ocean (occasionally 20–25 feet out east), 7–10 feet on Long Island Sound and around 10 feet on western Block Island Sound, with gales possibly continuing into Friday.
watch_for: Widespread minor to moderate, locally major, coastal flooding on Thursday with king tides and the full moon.
Thanksgiving winds gusting 35–45 mph, possibly 50 mph at the coast, strongest Thursday afternoon and evening.
Rain totals of 1–2 inches Thursday, with a 20–30 percent chance of more than 2.5 inches near the coast.
confidence: Forecasters see no significant changes and are confident in a warm Monday and cold, dry Tuesday and Wednesday, with continued confidence in a large Thanksgiving coastal storm, though its exact track and timing (recently slowed a bit) still affect rain and wind details.
